q1: SELECT CUSTOMER_ID FROM CUSTOMER GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) FROM PRODUCT)
q2: SELECT C.CUSTOMER_ID FROM CUSTOMER C GROUP BY C.CUSTOMER_ID HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT C.PRODUCT_KEY) = (SELECT COUNT(*) AS COUNT FROM PRODUCT)
q1_prompt_sql: SELECT CUSTOMER_ID FROM CUSTOMER GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) FROM PRODUCT)
q2_prompt_sql: SELECT C.CUSTOMER_ID FROM CUSTOMER C GROUP BY C.CUSTOMER_ID HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT C.PRODUCT_KEY) = (SELECT COUNT(*) AS COUNT FROM PRODUCT)
counterexample: INSERT INTO PRODUCT (PRODUCT_KEY) VALUES (1), (2); INSERT INTO CUSTOMER (CUSTOMER_ID, PRODUCT_KEY) VALUES (1, 1), (2, 1), (3, 1);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent because Q1 uses COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) in the HAVING clause, while Q2 uses COUNT(*) AS COUNT in the subquery. This difference in the subquery's count function affects the results when the number of products is not the same as the number of distinct product keys.
counterexample_dsp: The difference is triggered when the number of products is not the same as the number of distinct product keys. This can happen if a product is associated with multiple customers.
